paper_title: Each Reward to Its Relevant Tokens: Reward-Specific Token-Level Credit Assignment for Multi-Reward RL

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Language models are increasingly trained against several verifiable rewards at once, such as the correctness and the format of a tool call, or the individual constraints of a complex instruction. Reward-decoupled normalization (GDPO) normalizes each reward separately so that different reward combinations keep distinct advantages, but it still spreads every reward's advantage evenly over the whole response, although each verifier checks only a few positions. We propose MRTPO, which assigns the advantage of each reward to the tokens relevant to it, using the information its verifier checks, without auxiliary models or token-level annotations. For each reward, the policy replays its own response with and without that reward's verifier information, and the per-token Jensen-Shannon distance between the two next-token distributions measures each token's relevance and reassigns the advantage. On text-to-SQL, multi-constraint instruction following and tool calling, MRTPO converges faster and achieves better performance than the compared methods.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Language models are increasingly trained against several verifiable rewards at once, such as the correctness and the format of tool call, or the individual constraints of complex instruction. Reward-decoupled normalization (GDPO) normalizes each reward separately so that different reward combinations keep distinct advantages, but it still spreads every rewards advantage evenly over the whole response, although each verifier checks only few positions. We propose MRTPO, which assigns the advantage of each reward to the tokens relevant to it, using the information its verifier checks, without auxiliary models or token-level annotations. For each reward, the policy replays its own response with and without that rewards verifier information, and the per-token Jensen Shannon distance between the two next-token distributions measures each tokens relevance and reassigns the advantage. On text-to-SQL, multi-constraint instruction following and tool calling, MRTPO converges faster and achieves better performance than the compared methods.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become standard component of large language model (LLM) post-training, with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and its variants among the most widely adopted algorithms (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). Many practical objectives, however, involve multiple criteria. tool-using agent must emit well-formed call and also select the correct function and arguments (Qian et al., 2025); text-to-SQL model must produce query that both executes and returns the intended result (Ma et al., 2025); an instruction-following model must satisfy every constraint stated in the prompt (Zhou et al., 2023); and an aligned assistant must be both helpful and harmless (Dai et al., 2024). Each criterion is typically evaluated by separate verifier that produces its 1 Figure 1: Advantages assigned to the tokens of one SQL response that is well formed and executable but uses >= for >. MRTPO places format credit on the tags, executability credit on the query, and the execution penalty mostly on >= 30. own reward, which gives rise to multi-reward reinforcement learning (Liu et al., 2026b). Applying GRPO to the sum of these rewards collapses distinct reward combinations into identical advantage values (Liu et al., 2026b). To address this reward collapse, GDPO normalizes each reward within its rollout group before aggregation (Liu et al., 2026b), and line of concurrent work further adapts the weight of each reward during aggregation (Jiang et al., 2026; He et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026a; Montero et al., 2026). These methods determine how much each reward contributes to the response-level advantage, yet the resulting advantage is still assigned uniformly to every token of the response. This implicitly treats every token as equally responsible for every reward, whereas verifier typically evaluates only small portion of the response. For instance, if tool call specifies all arguments correctly but omits the required <think> tag, the format penalty is imposed equally on the correctly generated arguments. This motivates the following question: Can we identify the tokens relevant to each reward and assign the rewards advantage mainly to them? Recent work on on-policy self-distillation suggests an answer. Conditioning model on privileged information, such as reference solution or environment feedback, alters its next-token predictions on response it has already generated; selfdistillation methods train the policy to match these privileged predictions, thereby replacing reward maximization with distillation toward teacher distribution (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026). In multi-reward RL, such information is available separately for each reward, because every verifier holds the information it relies on for evaluation, such as reference tool call, the execution error of generated query, or an individual constraint of the instruction. Since this information decides the reward, we call token relevant to it when the information changes its prediction, and distribute the rewards advantage by this relevance. Building on this insight, we propose MRTPO (Multi-Reward-to-Token Policy Optimization), token-level credit assignment method for multireward RL. For each reward, MRTPO replays the sampled response under two contexts that differ only in the information of that rewards verifier, computes the token-wise JensenShannon distance between the resulting next-token distributions, and redistributes the group-normalized advantage of the reward across tokens according to this distance. This redistribution is what separates MRTPO from prior methods. GDPO (Liu et al., 2026b) and SAW (He et al., 2026) decide how much each reward contributes to response but give every token the same share, whereas MRTPO decides which tokens receive each rewards advantage. OPSD (Zhao et al., 2026) also uses privileged information and trains the policy to fit teacher that sees it. We highlight these differences in Figure 1. Our main contributions are as follows: credit-assignment perspective on multireward RL. We show that existing multi-reward methods determine the weight of each reward only at the response level and assign the advantage of every reward uniformly to all tokens, although only part of the response is relevant to each reward. Reward-specific token-level credit assignment. We propose MRTPO, which constructs context pairs from each verifiers own information and derives token weights for each reward separately through self-replay, requiring no auxiliary model, token-level annotation or additional generation. Experiments. Experiments on text-to-SQL, multi-constraint instruction following and tool calling show that MRTPO achieves higher performance than GDPO with faster convergence.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Multi-reward reinforcement learning. Early work on multi-objective alignment balances several objectives by training separate reward models or by interpolating policies trained on different rewards (Dai et al., 2024; Ramé et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023). Within the GRPO framework (Shao et al., 2024), the question becomes how to turn reward vector into group-relative advantages. GDPO normalizes each reward within its group before summation so that different reward combinations remain distinguishable (Liu et al., 2026b). Concurrent work builds on GDPO and adjusts the weight of each reward dynamically according to withingroup variance, training progress or conflicts between rewards (Jiang et al., 2026; He et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026a; Montero et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026). All of these methods operate at the response level. Different from these approaches, MRTPO keeps the reward-wise group advantages of GDPO and further decides which tokens receive each rewards advantage, so it can be combined with any of these reweighting methods, as we do with SAW in Section 5.1. Token-level credit assignment and privileged information. To obtain credit finer than responselevel advantage, prior work relies on process reward models (Lightman et al., 2024), Monte-Carlo value estimates (Kazemnejad et al., 2025) or tokenlevel discriminators trained for each rubric item (Xu et al., 2026), which require step-level annotations, additional sampling or an additional model. Other methods derive token weights from token entropy (Wang et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a) or from replaying the response without the entire rubric (Zhang et al., 2026a), but they reweight the aggregated advantage rather than each reward separately. Another line of work uses privileged information for on-policy self-distillation. Given reference solution or environment feedback, the same model acts as the teacher, and the student fits the distribution of the teacher (Agarwal et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026). MRTPO also builds on privileged information and 2 self-replay, and uses the distributional difference under each rewards information to allocate that rewards advantage over tokens. The rewards thus remain the training objective, and the replay only decides where each advantage goes.

sections.title: 4.1 Motivation
sections.content: Because every token shares one advantage (Eq. 3), the penalty for an error is spread over the whole response and can be outweighed by the credit of other rewards. In Figure 2, only the selected column is wrong, yet GDPO credits the entire query, the wrong column included. Each reward is decided by few tokens, here the execution reward by the selected column. MRTPO finds the tokens relevant to each reward (Section 4.2) and places the rewards advantage mainly on them (Section 4.3).

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate MRTPO on three settings: text-toSQL, instruction following and tool calling. The complete training and evaluation parameters are given in Appendix B, and the prompts and verifier blocks in Appendix C. Text-to-SQL. Given question and database schema, the model reasons in <think> and writes SQL query in <answer>. We train on the Spider training set (Yu et al., 2018) with three binary rewards following SQL-R1 (Ma et al., 2025): format, executability and execution match against the reference query. The verifier blocks of MRTPO state the required format, the SQLite error raised by the responses own query, and the reference query. We train Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct and 7B-Instruct (Hui et al., 2024) for 100 steps and report greedy execution accuracy, the fraction of questions whose query returns the same result as the reference, on Spider dev and test, Spider-Syn (Gan et al., 2021a), Spider-Realistic (Deng et al., 2021), Spider-DK (Gan et al., 2021b) and BIRD dev (Li et al., 2023). Instruction following. We train on the first two subsets of HIR-16K (Zhang et al., 2026b), whose constraints are programmatically verifiable. All metrics are averaged over five samples per prompt. Tool calling. Following ToolRL (Qian et al., 2025), the model selects tools and fills in their arguments. We train on the RLLA data with format reward and correctness reward that compares tool names, parameter names and values with the reference calls. The verifier blocks of MRTPO state the required format and list the reference calls. We train Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and 3B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024) for 100 steps and report the official AST accuracy on the single-turn Non-Live and Live categories of BFCL-v4 (Patil et al., 2025). Baselines. On all tasks we compare with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and GDPO (Liu et al., 2026b). Most concurrent multi-reward methods reweight the rewards when aggregating them; we select SAW (He et al., 2026) as their representative. Since reweighting is orthogonal to MRTPO, we compare with SAW on top of GDPO and also apply it on top of MRTPO. On instruction following the rewards differ across prompts, so such reweighting does not apply, and we instead compare with CoRT (Zhang et al., 2026a), token-level method. On text-to-SQL, where reference reasoning chains are available (Li et al., 2025), we also compare with onpolicy self-distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026). MRTPO uses β = 0.5 on all tasks, and all results are averaged over independent training runs.

sections.title: 5.2 Main Results
sections.content: Does token-level assignment improve multireward RL? MRTPO has the best average performance on all three tasks and all six models (Tables 1, 2 and 3). MRTPO and GDPO compute the same per-reward advantages and differ only in how each advantage is assigned to the tokens, so the improvement comes from the token-level assignment 6 Figure 5: Training dynamics. (a) Text-to-SQL execution accuracy averaged over six benchmarks (Qwen2.5-Coder7B-Instruct); (b) training response length (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct); (c, d) IFBench prompt-level and MulDimIF accuracy (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507). Lines are seed means; bands span the seeds. Figure 6: Where the replay distance falls. (a, b) Text-to-SQL with Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct; (c, d) tool calling with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. (a, c) Share of each rewards distance held by the top tokens of response; (b, d) share on each part of the response. Gray marks the uniform assignment of GDPO. alone. MRTPO is orthogonal to response-level reweighting such as SAW and still outperforms it on text-to-SQL. Combined with SAW, it gives the best average with both models. OPSD gives its teacher more privileged information than MRTPO receives, full reference solution with the reasoning and the query, yet it stays below MRTPO on every text-to-SQL benchmark. This shows that the policy needs only the information its verifiers already use, not full reference solution. When does it help most? The gain grows with the number of rewards in response. Under uniform assignment every token receives the sum of all rewards advantages, so most of the credit on token comes from rewards unrelated to it, and this share grows with the number of rewards. Instruction following has five to thirteen constraint rewards per prompt, and here MRTPO gains most, 2.4 and 3.2 points on IFBench, whose constraints are not seen in training. Text-to-SQL has three rewards, and MRTPO gains 1.3 and 1.6 points in average accuracy. Tool calling has two, and MRTPO ends close to GDPO; its gain there is in speed. Does it learn faster? reward decided by few tokens receives only small share of its advantage on those tokens when the advantage is spread uniformly. The format reward of tool calling, which its verifier checks on the tags alone, shows this most clearly. After 10 steps, MRTPO produces the required format on 97% of the BFCL cases, compared with 2% for GDPO and 4% for GRPO (Figure 4d). The other tasks show the same pattern. With Coder-7B, MRTPO passes the final text-toSQL accuracy of GDPO at step 60 of 100, and with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 it passes the final IFBench accuracy of every baseline at step 200 of 300 (Figure 5a, c). In text-to-SQL the responses also become 40% shorter than those of GDPO with Coder-3B (Figure 5b), because reasoning that does not affect the query gets less execution advantage. Which tokens receive each rewards advantage? Without step-level annotations, the replay finds the tokens that decide each reward from forward passes of the policy itself (Figure 6). In text-to-SQL, 80% of rewards distance falls on 26% to 29% of the tokens (Figure 6a). The execution reward puts 10% of its distance on the selected columns, twice their share of the tokens, and little on the tags, while the format reward puts twice their share on the tags (Figure 6b). Replaying all rewards together assigns their summed advantage with one shared profile. It improves over GDPO but stays below MRTPO, so the gain also depends on giving each reward its own assignment. We set β = 0.5 on all tasks instead of tuning it per task. On two tasks we also tried 0.25 and 0.75 (Tables 6 and 7). On instruction following, 0.5 gives the highest IFBench accuracy and average, while 0.75 is higher on IFEval and MulDimIF; on text-to-SQL, 0.25 gives slightly higher average. The best β thus depends on the task, and tuning it per task could improve MRTPO further, which we leave aside because of its compute cost. What does the replay cost? Replay adds forward passes of the policy. For each reward, MRTPO replays response only when that reward varies within its group, since otherwise its advantage is zero. Such groups are common only early in training and quickly become rare: in tool calling, the share of groups whose correctness varies falls from 61% in the first ten steps to about 10%. Overall, 12% to 21% of the responsereward pairs are replayed, and training step takes 10% to 20% longer than with GDPO on the same GPUs.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce MRTPO, which tells multi-reward learner not only which rewards response earned but also which tokens earned each of them. The key idea of MRTPO is to replay the policys own response under the prompt with and without one verifiers information, such as reference query, an execution error or constraint. The tokens whose predictions change most are the ones this reward depends on, and MRTPO assigns more of the rewards advantage to them, without step-level annotations. Across text-to-SQL, instruction following and tool calling, MRTPO consistently outperforms GRPO and GDPO on six models and reaches the final accuracy of GDPO in fewer steps. Any reward that comes with checkable information, such as reference answer, an execution error or rubric item, can be assigned to its tokens this way.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: MRTPO requires that each rewards verification information can be written as text and that adding or removing it changes the predictions from the policy. Rewards without such information, for example response length, cannot be localized this way and shall keep uniform allocation in GDPO. Our experiments use models of 1.5B to 7B parameters with single allocation strength (β = 0.5) on all tasks. Larger models, rewards judged by an LLM such as rubric items, and adaptive choices of β remain to be studied.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: This work studies credit assignment for reinforcement learning on publicly available text-to-SQL, instruction-following and tool-calling datasets with programmatic verifiers. It does not involve human subjects or new data collection. More efficient optimization of verifiable rewards also makes it easier to optimize misspecified rewards.

sections.title: A Relation to Reweighting Methods
sections.content: Algorithm 1 compares one training step of GDPO and MRTPO. Most concurrent multi-reward methods change only how the per-reward advantages are combined into one advantage per response. They weight each reward by batch or group statistics, mask or weight responses, or replace the sum with soft minimum, and every token of response receives the same advantage  (Table 8)  . MRTPO instead changes how each advantage is assigned to the tokens, so it is orthogonal to all of these methods. In this paper we combine it with SAW as an example  (Table 1)  .

GRPO standardizes the aggregated reward within each group, without batch-level rescaling. Text-to-SQL. We drop 3 Spider training questions whose reference query fails to execute and 82 whose prompt exceeds 4,096 tokens. The reference solutions of OPSD are the chain-of-thought solutions that OmniSQL releases for the Spider training set. OPSD shares the rollout and optimizer settings of the other methods, and its teacher is the initial model whose context shows the reference solution as an earlier answer to the same question, followed by the original prompt. For SAW, each rewards group advantage is multiplied by its coefficient of variation in the batch, normalized so that the three weights sum to three. Instruction following. We use the first two subsets of HIR-16K, 6,998 prompts with 43,496 constraints, because all their constraints are checked by programs, while the other subsets need an LLM judge. Tool calling. We follow the public GDPO implementation. Reference argument values written as numeric or boolean strings are converted to the types declared in the tool schema.
